learn.b: TypeScript is JavaScript with types added on top. You write types to describe your data, and a checker finds mistakes before the program runs. Every valid JavaScript program is also valid TypeScript.
learn.code:
let age: number = 15;
age = "fifteen"; // Error: string is not a number

learn.b: Browsers and Node run JavaScript, not TypeScript. The compiler tsc reads .ts files, checks the types and writes .js files. Types are erased in the output, so they cost nothing when the program runs.
learn.code:
// install once
npm install -g typescript

tsc hello.ts   // makes hello.js
node hello.js

learn.b: A TypeScript file looks like JavaScript with annotations after names. A colon followed by a type says what a variable can hold. Many types are worked out automatically, which is called type inference.

If the types do not match, tsc reports an error with the file name and line number. By default it still creates the .js file, but you should fix the errors first. Editors like VS Code show the same errors as red underlines while you type.
learn.code:
let n: number = 5;
n.toUpperCase(); // Error: Property does not exist on type number

learn.b: The main simple types are string, number, boolean, null and undefined. There is only one number type for both whole numbers and decimals. Write the type after the name with a colon. Use lowercase type names.

any turns the type checker off for that value, so avoid it. unknown is the safe version: you must check the value before using it. void is the return type of a function that returns nothing, and never is for things that cannot happen, like a function that always throws.

If you give a variable a value when you declare it, TypeScript guesses the type for you. A const with a plain value gets a very specific type, like the exact text "hi". Annotate only when inference cannot know the type.
learn.code:
let a = 5;        // number
const b = "hi";   // type is "hi"
let c;            // implicit any

learn.b: With strictNullChecks (part of strict mode) a variable cannot be null or undefined unless you say so. Write a union like string | null to allow it. Turning strict on is recommended because it catches many bugs.

qs.why: TypeScript has one number type.

qs.why: unknown forces you to check before use.

learn.b: An array type is the item type followed by []. You can also write Array<number>. Every item must have that type, so mixing types gives an error. The usual methods like push, map and filter are all type checked.
Reading an item gives you the item type. A for...of loop goes through the values, and TypeScript knows the type of each one. map returns a new array whose type comes from your function.
A tuple is an array with a fixed length where each position has its own type. Write the types in square brackets. Use a tuple for a small group of different things, like a name and an age.
Add readonly to stop an array or tuple from being changed. You can pull values out of an array or tuple with destructuring, and the types follow along. Tuple items can also be optional or have names.

qs.q: How do you write the type of an array of strings?
qs.why: The item type followed by [].

o: A fixed-length array with a type for each position
qs.why: Each position in a tuple has its own type.

const r = nums.map(n => String(n));
qs.why: map returns an array of the callback's return type.

learn.b: Write a type after each parameter and after the closing parenthesis for the return type. Callers must pass the right number and types of arguments. If you leave the return type out, TypeScript infers it.
A question mark makes a parameter optional, and its type then includes undefined. A default value also makes a parameter optional. Optional parameters must come after the required ones.
Arrow functions are typed the same way. A function type describes a function's shape: the parameters, then an arrow, then the return type. Use it for callbacks and for variables that hold functions.

A rest parameter collects extra arguments into an array, so its type is an array. Overloads declare several allowed call shapes before one real implementation. Functions that never return a value are typed void.

o: After the parentheses with a colon

qs.why: name?: string makes the argument optional.

qs.why: Optional parameters must come last.

learn.b: You can describe an object's shape by listing its properties and their types. TypeScript checks that every property exists and has the right type. An extra or missing property is an error when you create the object.

An interface gives a name to an object shape so you can reuse it. By convention the name starts with a capital letter. Anything that has the right properties fits the interface, even without saying so.
Add ? after a property name to make it optional. Add readonly in front to stop it from being changed after the object is made. Interfaces can also describe methods.

An interface can extend another one to add more properties. It keeps everything from the parent. An interface can also describe a function or an object with any number of keys using an index signature.

qs.q: Which keyword creates a reusable object shape?
qs.why: interface names an object shape.

qs.q: What does note?: string mean in an interface?
qs.why: The question mark makes the property optional.

qs.q: What happens here?
qs.code:

const u: User = { name: "Ana" };
qs.why: The object lacks the required age property.

qs.why: readonly blocks reassignment.

learn.b: A type alias gives a name to any type using the type keyword. It works for objects, unions, tuples and more. Aliases make long types short and readable.
A union type allows one of several types, written with a pipe. A variable of type string | number can hold either, but you can only use what both types share until you check which one it is.
A literal type is one exact value, like "left" or 3. Combine literals in a union to list the only allowed values. This is great for options and states because typos become errors.

An intersection with & combines types so a value has all their properties. A discriminated union is a union of objects that share a literal property such as kind, which tells you which one you have. This pattern makes state handling safe.

qs.why: type Name = ... creates an alias.

qs.why: | makes a union and & makes an intersection.

learn.b: With a union you can only use members that every type has. Narrowing means checking the type so TypeScript knows which one you have in that block. After the check you can use the full features of that type.
A typeof check on a primitive narrows the type inside the if. A truthiness check removes null and undefined. The else branch gets the remaining types.

The in operator checks if a property exists on an object. instanceof checks if an object comes from a class. Comparing with === to a literal also narrows. Optional chaining ?. and nullish ?? help with values that may be missing.

When objects share a literal property like kind, checking it narrows to the exact member. A switch on kind is ideal. You can also write a type predicate function that returns x is Type to make your own guard.

o: Checking a type so TypeScript knows which it is
qs.why: Narrowing refines a union to one type.

qs.q: What is the type of x in the else branch?
qs.why: The string case was removed, leaving number.

learn.b: Sometimes a function should work with any type but keep track of it. Using any loses the type. A generic uses a type parameter, like T, as a placeholder that is filled in when you call the function.
You can let TypeScript infer T, or you can write it yourself in angle brackets. A function can have more than one type parameter. Names are usually T, U, K and V.
Use extends to limit what T can be. This lets you use certain properties inside the function. Only types that have those properties are accepted.
Interfaces, type aliases and classes can be generic too. Built in types like Array<T>, Promise<T> and Map<K, V> use this idea. You choose the type when you create the object.

qs.q: What is T in function first<T>(a: T[]): T?
qs.why: T is a placeholder for a type.

qs.q: Why use generics instead of any?
qs.why: A generic remembers the type that was passed in.

qs.q: What type does r have?
qs.code:
function first<T>(a: T[]): T { return a[0]; }
const r = first([5, 6]);
qs.why: first receives number[], so T becomes number.

qs.q: A generic function can have more than one type parameter.
qs.why: For example <A, B>.

learn.b: A class has typed properties, a constructor and methods. You must declare the properties with their types. Create objects with new, just like in JavaScript.
public is the default and means anyone can use it. private means only code inside the class. protected means the class and its children. These are checked at compile time only.

You can put a modifier on a constructor parameter to declare and assign the property in one step. readonly stops a property from being changed after the constructor. This removes a lot of repeated code.

extends makes a class inherit from another, and super calls the parent constructor. implements checks that a class follows an interface. An abstract class cannot be created directly and can have abstract methods that children must write. static members belong to the class itself.

qs.q: Which modifier hides a member from outside the class?
qs.why: private is only usable inside the class.

qs.q: Which modifier allows the class and its subclasses?
qs.why: protected is shared with child classes.

qs.q: What happens on the last line?
qs.why: A private member cannot be read outside the class.

qs.q: public is the default access modifier in TypeScript classes.
qs.why: Members are public unless you say otherwise.

learn.b: An enum is a named set of related values. Without values, members count from 0. A string enum gives each member a text value. Use const enum or a union of literals if you want smaller output.
Utility types transform existing types. Partial makes every property optional, Required makes them all required, and Readonly makes them all read-only. They save you from rewriting shapes.
Pick keeps only the listed properties and Omit removes them. Record builds an object type from key and value types. keyof gives the property names of a type as a union.

A tsconfig.json file configures the compiler. Run tsc --init to create one, then just run tsc. Important options are target for the JavaScript version, outDir for the output folder, and strict to turn on all strict checks. Also useful are include, rootDir and noImplicitAny.

qs.q: What number does the first member of an enum get by default?
qs.why: Enum members count from 0.

qs.q: Which utility type makes every property optional?
qs.why: Partial<T> makes all properties optional.

qs.q: What does Omit<User, "age"> produce?

interface User { name: string; age: number }
type T = Omit<User, "age">;
qs.why: Omit removes the listed keys.
